{"kind":"proof","text":"Let a potential triple be any three consecutive cells in one row or column. A collection of removed blocks is terminal only if every potential triple contains a removed cell.

For \(n\ge3\), there are \(2n(n-2)\) potential triples. A horizontal removed block intersects at most five horizontal potential triples, since their starting columns lie within two positions of the block’s starting column. Each of its three cells belongs to at most three vertical potential triples, so the block intersects at most nine vertical triples. Thus each removed block intersects at most \(14\) potential triples; the same argument applies to a vertical block.

Consequently, if a terminal collection contains \(k\) blocks, then
\[
14k\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
and hence
\[
b(n)\ge \frac{n(n-2)}7=\frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For \(n=1,2\), we have \(b(n)=0\), and the same inequality holds. Thus we may take \(c=2/7\).

For the upper bound, consider the infinite square lattice. In every row \(r\), place horizontal three-cell blocks beginning at every column \(s\) satisfying
\[
r+s\equiv0\pmod5.
\]
Blocks in a fixed row have starting columns five apart, so all these blocks are pairwise disjoint. Their occupied cells form
\[
D=\{(r,q):r+q\pmod5\in\{0,1,2\}\}.
\]
Every horizontal triple meets \(D\), since three consecutive residues modulo \(5\) cannot all lie in the complement \(\{3,4\}\). The same reasoning, varying the row coordinate, shows that every vertical triple meets \(D\).

Now let \(n\ge6\) and restrict the construction to the \(n\times n\) board. Retain every periodic block lying entirely inside the board. In each row, if a periodic block meets the board but extends past the left edge, add the block in columns \(1,2,3\). If one extends past the right edge, add the block in columns \(n-2,n-1,n\).

These blocks remain disjoint. A periodic block crossing the left edge starts at column \(-1\) or \(0\), so the next periodic block starts at \(4\) or \(5\), beyond the added block in columns \(1,2,3\). The right-edge argument is symmetric, and the two boundary blocks are disjoint because \(n\ge6\). Every cell of \(D\) inside the board is therefore removed: its unique periodic block is either retained or its portion inside the board is covered by a boundary block. Since every horizontal or vertical triple meets \(D\), no triple remains after these removals.

Each row contains at most \(n/5+1\) retained periodic blocks and at most two boundary blocks. Thus the number of removed blocks is at most
\[
n\left(\frac n5+3\right)=\frac15n^2+3n.
\]
For \(1\le n\le5\), greedily remove available blocks until none remains. Since the blocks are disjoint, at most \(n^2/3\) blocks are removed, and
\[
\frac{n^2}{3}\le \frac{n^2}{5}+3n
\]
for these values of \(n\). Hence the upper bound holds for every positive integer \(n\) with \(d=3\).

Therefore, for all positive integers \(n\),
\[
\frac17n^2-\frac27n\le b(n)\le\frac15n^2+3n,
\]
which proves the theorem.","reason":"The potential-triple count gives the lower bound, while the disjoint period-five construction and its controlled boundary correction give a terminal configuration with the required upper-bound size."}

{"problem": {"theorem": "I have an \(n \times n\) sheet of stamps, from which I've been asked to tear out blocks of three adjacent stamps in a single row or column. (I can only tear along the perforations separating adjacent stamps, and each block must come out of the sheet in one piece.) Let \(b(n)\) be the smallest number of blocks I can tear out and make it impossible to tear out any more blocks. Prove that there are real constants \(c\) and \(d\) such that

\[
\frac{1}{7} n^{2}-c n \leq b(n) \leq \frac{1}{5} n^{2}+d n
\]

for all \(n>0\).", "assumptions": [], "domain": "usamo", "proof_text": "Proof.  We think of the final “blocked’’ configuration as the result of tearing out \(b(n)\) disjoint 3-stamp blocks (each block either 3 in a row or 3 in a column) so that no further 3-stamp block remains.  Call any three consecutive positions in a row or in a column a “potential triple.’’  There are in all  
\[
H \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{horizontal triples,}
\qquad
V \;=\; n\,(n-2)
\quad\text{vertical triples,}
\]
and hence 
\[
T \;=\;H+V \;=\;2\,n\,(n-2)
\]
potential triples that must each be “hit’’ (i.e.\ each must lose at least one stamp) by our removed blocks.

1.  Lower bound \(b(n)\ge \tfrac1{7}n^2-cn\).  
 
Fix any one of the \(b(n)\) removed blocks.  If it is a horizontal block occupying cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\), then it “hits’’ (i.e.\ destroys at least one cell of) at most
  •  all horizontal triples that include one of those three cells;  in a row of length \(n\), each interior cell lies in 3 horizontal triples and each end‐cell in 1 or 2, and one checks easily that the three consecutive cells \((i,j),(i,j+1),(i,j+2)\) together lie in at most 5 distinct horizontal triples;  
  •  all vertical triples that include one of those three cells;  each of the three removed stamps lies in at most 3 vertical triples, so altogether at most \(3\times3=9\) vertical triples.  
Hence that one horizontal block can destroy at most \(5+9=14\) of the \(T\) potential triples.  Likewise any vertical block destroys at most \(14\) potential triples.  

Since in the final configuration every one of the \(T=2n(n-2)\) potential triples must be destroyed by at least one of the removed blocks, and since each block can destroy at most \(14\) triples, we get the inequality
\[
14\,b(n)\;\ge\;2\,n(n-2)\;=\;2n^2-4n,
\]
i.e.
\[
b(n)\;\ge\;\frac{2n^2-4n}{14}
\;=\;\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}\,n.
\]
Thus the stated lower bound holds with \(c=\tfrac{2}{7}\).

2.  Upper bound \(b(n)\le \tfrac1{5}n^2+dn\).

We give an explicit “tiling’’ construction with density \(1/5\), up to an \(O(n)\) boundary correction.  Assume for simplicity that \(n\) is a multiple of 5; the leftover strip of width \(<5\) on the right and top can then be handled by at most \(O(n)\) extra blocks without changing the leading term.

Partition the \(n\times n\) grid into \(\tfrac n5\times\tfrac n5\) little \(5\times5\) macrosquares.  In each \(5\times5\) macro with local coordinates \((r,c)\), \(1\le r,c\le5\), remove exactly the following 5 blocks (each of size 3):

  A)  A horizontal block in row \(r=2\), columns \(c=1,2,3\).

  B)  A horizontal block in row \(r=4\), columns \(c=3,4,5\).

  C)  A vertical block in column \(c=2\), rows \(r=3,4,5\).

  D)  A vertical block in column \(c=4\), rows \(r=1,2,3\).

  E)  A horizontal block in row \(r=5\), columns \(c=2,3,4\).

One checks by an easy (though a bit tedious) case‐by‐case verification that in this repeated pattern every horizontal triple of three consecutive stamps in any row will contain at least one removed stamp (from one of the above horizontal blocks in its macro or in an adjacent macro), and similarly every vertical triple of three consecutive stamps in any column meets one of the vertical blocks C) or D).  Thus after tearing out these \(5\) blocks in each \(5\times5\) cell there is no triple left anywhere in the \(n\times n\) square.

Since there are \(\tfrac n5\) macros in each direction, the total number of blocks used is
\[
5\;\times\;\Bigl(\frac n5\Bigr)^2
\;=\;\frac15\,n^2.
\]
Adding the \(O(n)\) extra blocks needed to cover the final partial strips (of width \(<5\)) along the top and right edges gives
\[
b(n)\;\le\;\frac15\,n^2 \;+\;O(n).
\]
Hence the upper bound holds with some constant \(d\).

Combining (1) and (2) completes the proof: for all \(n>0\),
\[
\frac1{7}\,n^2-\frac{2}{7}n\;\le\;b(n)\;\le\;\frac1{5}\,n^2+d\,n,
\]
as required.  ∎", "explicit_subgoals": []}, "rule_candidates": [{"id": "grp_normal_quotient", "name": "Quotient group criterion", "statement": "If N is a normal subgroup of G, then the set of left cosets G/N forms a group under (aN)(bN) = abN.", "conditions": ["N is a subgroup of G", "N is normal in G"], "conclusion": "G/N is a group and coset multiplication is well-defined.", "rule_digest": "f6d458aa2e7463efeea7a535cdbe0f0f7930259cfe7f845b5350ec03454da876", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "ring_quotient_ideal", "name": "Quotient ring criterion", "statement": "If I is a two-sided ideal of a ring R, then R/I is a quotient ring with operations defined on cosets.", "conditions": ["I is a two-sided ideal of R"], "conclusion": "R/I is a ring and coset operations are well-defined.", "rule_digest": "5c419f063bbc02eba57c0943d5ecce5f2e4c1b370cbb5ad6d69c2e08c3b21835", "applicability": "unchecked"}, {"id": "grp_first_iso", "name": "First isomorphism theorem for groups", "statement": "If phi: G -> H is a group homomorphism, then G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "conditions": ["phi is a group homomorphism", "ker(phi) is the kernel of phi"], "conclusion": "G/ker(phi) is isomorphic to im(phi).", "rule_digest": "335c687d26f64e41584f1b8bc575aec9d78223b01c4821bf0056bf8533de0c19", "applicability": "unchecked"}], "draft": "Let a potential triple be any three consecutive cells in one row or column. Its three cells meet at most three vertical triples each, hence at most nine vertical triples. Thus it meets at most 14 potential triples. The same holds for a vertical block. Consequently every terminal collection of k blocks satisfies
\[
14k\ge 2n(n-2),
\]
so
\[
b(n)\ge \frac17n^2-\frac27n.
\]
For n=1,2 this inequality also holds, since b(n)=0. Thus we may take c=2/7.

For the upper bound, first define a periodic packing of the infinite square lattice. In row r, place horizontal blocks beginning at every column s satisfying
\[

\]
The blocks in each row are separated by two cells and are therefore disjoint. Their union is exactly
\[

\]
Every horizontal triple meets D, because among three consecutive residues modulo 5 at least one belongs to \(\{0,1,2\}\). The same argument, with the row coordinate varying, shows that every vertical triple meets D.

In each row, if a periodic block intersects the left edge without being contained in the board, add the horizontal block in columns 1,2,3. Likewise, if a periodic block intersects the right edge without being contained, add the block in columns n-2,n-1,n.

These added blocks are disjoint from the retained blocks. Indeed, a block crossing the left edge starts at -1 or 0, so the next periodic block starts at 4 or 5; the right-edge case is symmetric. The two added boundary blocks are disjoint because n≥6. \]

Terminality is correctly translated into hitting every length-three row or column segment. Each removed block intersects at most 14 such segments, giving the stated lower bound. The periodic horizontal packing is disjoint, its occupied set meets every horizontal and vertical triple, and the boundary modifications remain disjoint while covering all occupied lattice cells inside the board.
